examples.question_text:
Construct the network diagram for this project. Durations are in hours.

| Activity | Duration | Immediate predecessors |
|---|---:|---|
| A | 3 | — |
| B | 4 | — |
| C | 2 | A |
| D | 5 | B |
| E | 6 | C, D |
| F | 2 | E |

Construct a network diagram for the project, clearly identifying both dummy activities. Durations are in minutes.

| Activity | Duration | Immediate predecessors |
|---|---:|---|
| A | 7 | — |
| B | 4 | — |
| C | 6 | — |
| D | 8 | A, B |
| E | 9 | B, C |

examples.solution_text:
$A$ and $B$ leave Start, so neither has an immediate predecessor.

$C$ starts where $A$ ends. $D$ starts where $B$ ends, but the dummy also brings the dependency on $A$ to that vertex. Therefore, $D$ needs both $A$ and $B$.

$E$ follows $C$, and $F$ follows $D$. Record the real activities only; the dummy passes a dependency and has no separate activity row.

| Activity | Duration (minutes) | Immediate predecessors |
|---|---:|---|
| A | 4 | — |
| B | 7 | — |
| C | 2 | A |
| D | 6 | A, B |
| E | 5 | C |
| F | 3 | D |

examples.question_text:
Which network description matches this precedence table? Durations are in days. Every description uses these durations as edge labels and joins all final activities to one Finish vertex.

| Activity | Duration | Immediate predecessors |
|---|---:|---|
| A | 6 | — |
| B | 4 | — |
| C | 3 | A |
| D | 7 | A, B |
| E | 2 | C |

A. $A$ and $B$ leave Start. $C$ follows $A$ only. A dummy runs from the end of $A$ to the end of $B$, where $D$ starts. $E$ follows $C$.

B. $A$ and $B$ leave Start and end at one shared vertex, where both $C$ and $D$ start. $E$ follows $C$.

C. $A$ and $B$ leave Start. $C$ follows $A$ only. A dummy runs from the end of $B$ to the end of $A$, where $C$ starts. $D$ follows $B$ only. $E$ follows $C$.
examples.solution_text:
Check each activity's starting vertex against its predecessor list.

Description A makes $C$ depend on $A$ only and $D$ depend on both $A$ and $B$ through the dummy. It also places $E$ after $C$.

Description B incorrectly makes $C$ wait for $B$ as well as $A$.

Description C reverses the dummy: it adds $B$ as a predecessor of $C$ and leaves $D$ dependent on $B$ only.

Correct answer: A.

examples.derivation: Independently traced the diagram: A and B leave Start; C follows A; D follows B; C and D terminate at the start of E; F follows E and terminates at Finish. All six duration labels match the table. The branching and merging construction follows the supplied booklet method; no dummy or time calculation is needed.

Independently traced both dummy paths from the end of B. The upper junction receives A directly and B through a dummy, giving D exactly A and B as predecessors. The lower junction receives C directly and B through a dummy, giving E exactly B and C. Neither junction receives the other branch's dependency. All five real durations match, both dummies have zero duration, and D and E end at Finish. This adapts the booklet's two-dummy worked example.

Read the network independently: A has duration 4 and no predecessor; B has duration 7 and no predecessor; C has duration 2 and predecessor A; D has duration 6 and predecessors A and B because the dummy runs from A's end to D's start; E has duration 5 and predecessor C; F has duration 3 and predecessor D. These entries exactly match the solution table. Omitting a separate dummy activity row follows the supplied source tasks.

The incomplete diagram already represents every listed dependency except A preceding D. A ends at P and D starts at Q, so the required zero-duration dummy is directed P to Q. The completed diagram gives D predecessors A and B while preserving C's sole predecessor A, E following C, and F following D. All duration labels are preserved. This follows the booklet's supplied-network completion method.

Independently checked each description against the table. A preserves C following A only, D following A and B, and E following C. B merges A and B before C and therefore adds an unwanted dependency on B. C directs the dummy backwards, adding B before C and omitting A before D. Exactly one description is correct: A. Textual network descriptions preserve the accepted assessment method and introduce no additional skill.
